newsitem.title: USA: Clinton salutes baseball legend Jackie Robinson.
newsitem.headline: Clinton salutes baseball legend Jackie Robinson.

text.p: A half century to the day after Jackie Robinson shattered major league baseball's colour barrier, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday led a tribute to the great black athlete and civil rights pioneer.

It was on April 15, 1947, that Robinson debuted with the Brooklyn Dodgers in a season-opening game against the Boston Braves, becoming the first black American to play big league baseball in modern times.

Robinson, who died of a heart attack in 1972 at age 53, paved the way for a long line of black players like Willie Mays, Hank Aaron, Reggie Jackson and Ken Griffey, Jr. He is also credited with helping inspire the civil rights movement.

Clinton, less than 8 months old when Robinson began blazing a trail for better treatment of blacks, was to join Robinson's widow Rachel and dozens of baseball luminaries at a nighttime ceremony honouring the sports and civil rights hero.

The ceremony was to take place after the fifth inning of a game between the New York Mets and the Los Angeles Dodgers, the team that Robinson starred on for 10 years before it was transplanted to California in 1958.

"I was 10 years old before I ever got a television, and Jackie Robinson had two years in baseball. And I got to watch him on television. I still remember that," Clinton told students at a Brooklyn junior high school anti-smoking rally several hours before the game at Shea Stadium.

Clinton, who blasted cigarette companies during the rally for aiming their advertising at young people, said Robinson "had to deal with all the prejudice and all the insults and all the hatred ... all the time waiting for the chance" to show what he could do on the baseball diamond.

The New York trip was his first domestic outing since he underwent knee surgery on March 14 to repair a right knee tendon torn when he stumbled at the Florida home of golf pro Greg Norman. He is still using crutches.

Sandwiched between the anti-smoking rally and the Robinson tribute was a fund-raising luncheon for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Clinton, who has come under fire for his fund-raising tactics in last year's election campaign, has continued his fund-raising activities while calling for campaign financing reform.
The day Robinson broke into the big leagues, the Dodgers won the game 5-3 before an overflow crowd at Ebbets Field, which was torn down to make way for a housing project in 1960.

In the season that followed, he stoically endured a stream of insults from racist fans and players including some of his own teammates, but he went on to have such a brilliant career he won over many of those who had opposed him and was ultimately enshrined in baseball's Hall of Fame.

In an NBC Radio interview on the eve of the trip, Clinton boasted that the United States had made great progress in fighting racial discrimination since Robinson's history-making first major league game but said more needed to be done.

"There is no question that it's much better than it was 50 years ago," Clinton said, citing the eradication of legal discrimination and the growth of cross-racial contacts among ordinary people. But he added: "We never finished the job."
"I think that most Americans still don't have ... enough friends, true friends, across racial lines," Clinton said.
